source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: variation in replicability across samples and settings
finding: 28 classic and new findings were replicated in 125 samples. About half replicated and effects shrank a lot. Variation came more from the effect than from the sample or culture.
numbers: 15,305 participants, 36 countries. 15/28 (54%) significant at p<.05; 14/28 at p<.0001. Median d 0.60 original vs 0.15 replication. 9/28 (32%) reversed. Q test showed heterogeneity in 11/28 (39%).
limits: Covers many social psychology effects, not only heuristics. Online protocols.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a single published bias effect size. Expect shrinkage; build the schema on checks, not on assumed bias strength.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: variation in replicability across samples and settings (item 16, mental accounting framing, Tversky and Kahneman 1981 Study 10)
finding: The Tversky and Kahneman 1981 cheap-item/costly-item travel effect replicated but at a much smaller size.
numbers: Original N=181: 68% would travel to save $5 on a $15 item vs 29% on a $125 item (OR 4.96). Replication N=7,228: 49% vs 32%, d=0.40 (95% CI .35-.45), OR 2.06.
limits: Stimuli were updated for 2014 prices and items, in consultation with an original author.
agent_relevance: Direction holds across many countries; magnitude is about half. Treat the bias as real but modest.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: variation in replicability across samples and settings (item 9, incidental anchors, Critcher and Gilovich 2008)
finding: A numeric name (phone P97 vs P17) did not shift sales estimates in the large replication.
limits: Incidental, environmental anchors only. Explicit anchors are a different and more robust effect.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant numbers in a prompt may matter less than explicit numeric anchors. Test both separately in LLMs.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: variation in replicability across samples and settings (item 25, affect and risk, Rottenstreich and Hsee 2001)
finding: An affect-driven choice effect reversed in direction in the replication.
numbers: N=7,218: 47% chose the affectively attractive option when the outcome was unlikely vs 51% when certain; d=-0.08 (95% CI -0.13 to -0.03).
limits: One task from the wider prospect-theory family.
agent_relevance: Some intuitive-error effects are fragile to wording; do not hard-code them as guardrails.

source: Klein et al. (2014) Investigating variation in replicability: a Many Labs replication project
finding: Not opened (HTTP 403). Second-hand via Kuhberger 2023: risky-choice framing (Asian disease) replicated at d=0.60 across labs.
numbers: Framing d=0.60 as cited by Kuhberger (2023).
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Framing is among the most replicable heuristics-and-biases effects; a priority target for LLM tests.

source: Kuhberger (2023) A systematic review of risky-choice framing effects
finding: The risky-choice framing effect is robust at about d=0.60 across methods. About a quarter of people show no framing effect, and the author argues framing can be adaptive.
numbers: Kuhberger 1998 meta-analysis: >100 studies, ~30,000 people, d=0.31 uncorrected. Steiger and Kuhberger 2018 bias-corrected d=0.52 (range 0.16 to 0.91 across task variants). Many Labs 1 d=0.60. Im and Chen 2022: h=0.612, 100,000+ people, 49 countries. d=0.60 equals r=0.28. Classic Asian disease problem: ~75% pick the sure gain, ~75% pick the risky loss.
limits: Tasks differ, so there is no single true effect size. Review, so some numbers are second-hand.
agent_relevance: Framing invariance is a sound, testable check: ask the same problem in gain and loss frames and require the same answer.

source: Kuhberger (2023) section on attribute and message framing, same review
finding: Outside the classic risky-choice task, framing effects are small or inconsistent.
numbers: Message-framing meta-analyses: very small, mostly non-significant, about d=0.10 (O'Keefe and Jensen). Food attitudes/intentions meta (25 studies, 76 effects): overall d=0.47, attitudes d=0.82, intentions d=0.05. Loss aversion across 600+ estimates: lambda=1.955.
limits: Second-hand reporting of other meta-analyses.
agent_relevance: Do not generalise from the Asian disease problem to all framing. Effects on stated attitudes are bigger than on behavior intentions.

source: Berthet (2021) The measurement of individual differences in cognitive biases: a review and improvement
finding: Reliable measures exist for about a dozen biases, but composite bias scores are unreliable and there is no general bias factor.
numbers: Composite of 15 classic tasks: Cronbach alpha 0.484 (as cited). Composite of 13 tasks (Aczel 2015) also unreliable. Bias scores are only moderately correlated with cognitive ability. At least two latent factors; low correlations between biases.
limits: Review plus the author's own studies. Confirmation bias had no good measure before this work.
agent_relevance: Bias is not one trait. A single debias instruction cannot be expected to fix all biases at once; use per-bias checks.

source: Aczel et al. (2015) Measuring individual differences in decision biases: methodological considerations
finding: Different versions of the same bias task are not interchangeable, and 13-task composites have weak internal consistency.
numbers: Study 1 N=1,279, 13 tasks in two survey versions: split-half about 0.38 (Test 1), alpha below acceptable; factor structures differed between versions. Study 2 N=527, three versions of 7 biases: same pattern.
limits: Single-item tasks hurt reliability. Online samples.
agent_relevance: Bias susceptibility depends on cover story and response format. LLM bias results from one phrasing do not generalise; test paraphrases.

source: Aczel et al. (2015) Is it time for studying real-life debiasing? Analogical intervention
finding: Analogical-encoding training improved performance 4 weeks later only on statistical-principle biases. Awareness training and no training did not help.
numbers: N=154, 10 biases, pre-test and 4-week post-test. Gain only for the composite of statistical biases (sample size, base rate, regression to the mean, covariation).
limits: Small groups; one follow-up point; online.
agent_relevance: Debiasing that works is abstract, rule-like (statistical) and taught by comparison. Prefer a few worked analogical examples per rule over generic warnings.

source: Royal Society Open Science (2022) Can we shift belief in the Law of Small Numbers?
finding: Interactive sample-training helped on the training task but did not transfer to a quiz.
numbers: N=100 scientists and social scientists. 20% scored zero on sample-size items; only 2 got more than 4/6 right. Quiz did not improve after training. 38% said they learned to wait for larger samples.
limits: Bonus pay for correct answers. Training was a simulation without explicit instruction.
agent_relevance: Even trained scientists fail the law of small numbers; experience alone does not remove it. Require explicit computation for sample-size questions.

source: Cognitive reflection and rational choice (PMC13295265, 2026)
finding: Higher CRT scorers choose more rationally even where intuition is not misleading, with no qualitative process difference.
numbers: N=249, each did 250 probabilistic inference tasks and 16 risky choices. The same Parallel Constraint Satisfaction model fits low and high CRT; high CRT uses it more consistently.
limits: Supports an integrative, not two-system, dual-process view.
agent_relevance: The fast-bad versus slow-good split is too crude. Reflection mainly adds consistency, so repeated sampling and checks may matter more than a separate slow mode.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2022) Thinking fast and slow in large language models
finding: GPT-3 falls for CRT traps like humans, but ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mostly avoid them.
numbers: CRT correct: humans 38% (original study n=3,428 had 41%), GPT-3 davinci-003 5%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, GPT-4 96%. Intuitive (trap) answers: humans 55%, davinci-003 80%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, GPT-4 0%.
limits: CRT items are likely in training data. Semantic illusions also tested.
agent_relevance: Newer models do not show classic CRT biases, so naive bias tests may saturate. Use novel items.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2022), chain-of-thought ablation
finding: Chain-of-thought cuts trap answers sharply for a weaker model, but strong models do well even without it.
numbers: davinci-003 with a step-by-step prompt: correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29%. Forcing no reasoning: ChatGPT-3.5 correct change not significant; GPT-4 correct 95% to 88%, intuitive 0% to 10%.
limits: One task family.
agent_relevance: Let the model reason on trap-prone items, and verify with a program.

source: Malberg et al. (2024) A comprehensive evaluation of cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: All 30 tested biases were found in at least some of 20 LLMs. Most biases go in the human direction. Capability does not predict low bias.
numbers: 20 LLMs, 30 biases, 30,000 test cases (200 scenarios x 5 variants x 30 biases). Status quo and disposition effect were negative on average. Gemini 1.5 Pro least biased; larger OpenAI models somewhat more biased; Llama 3.1 1B oddly low.
limits: Bias metric depends on the generated templates.
agent_relevance: Bias must be measured per model; do not assume a stronger model is safer.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: LLMs show anchoring, framing, status quo, primacy and group attribution patterns in admissions decisions. Having the model rewrite its own prompt works better than awareness prompts.
numbers: 13,465 prompts. A reject framing led one model to admit 40.5% more students than a neutral frame. Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Self-help rewriting cut biased prompts to 0 for group attribution and framing in high-capacity models.
limits: Admissions task only. Few-shot debiasing sometimes made things worse.
agent_relevance: Rewrite-to-neutral then answer is a cheap debias operator, but it works only for large models.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024), awareness vs few-shot
finding: The be-mindful-not-to-be-biased instruction helped some biases (primacy) but not others, and few-shot examples could add new failures.
numbers: Awareness prompt made primacy answer distributions more uniform for Llama 2 and GPT-4; self-help did better.
limits: Effects differ by bias and by model.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on a generic warning instruction.

source: Sumita, Takeuchi, Kashima (2024) Cognitive biases in LLMs: a survey and mitigation experiments
finding: Two human debiasing methods were tried on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 for six biases. Social-perspective prompting (SoPro) did little; naming the bias (AwaRe) helped.
numbers: Biases: order, compassion fade, egocentric, bandwagon, attentional, verbosity. GPT-4 less biased than GPT-3.5. SoPro made bandwagon worse. AwaRe reduced bandwagon in both models.
limits: Needs the bias name in advance. Result tables not transcribed here.
agent_relevance: Named-bias warnings can work when the bias is known, but they do not scale to unknown biases.

source: Itzhak et al. (2023) Instructed to bias: instruction-tuned models exhibit emergent cognitive bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF add or amplify decoy, certainty and belief bias. GPT-4 had lower belief bias but a stronger decoy effect.
numbers: Pretrained vs tuned versions of GPT-3, Mistral, T5. Bias score runs from -1 to 1. Tuned models were more biased.
limits: Bias scores use option likelihoods for open models.
agent_relevance: Alignment training is a source of bias. Re-check after each model update.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 answered 12 of 12 standard vignettes correctly or with human-like mistakes, but small adversarial changes led to non-human errors.
numbers: 12 standard vignettes (Linda, cab, hospital and others) plus adversarial variants.
agent_relevance: Performance on textbook bias items may be memorisation; probe with perturbations.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? GPT-3.5
finding: GPT-3.5 showed anchoring, conjunction/availability, framing and endowment effects, like humans on the same prompts.
numbers: Four studies; Study 1 anchoring compared with 61 mTurk participants.
limits: Money prompts were hard because the model declines to answer.
agent_relevance: Language alone may produce these effects, so they may be inherited, not coded in.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) Balancing rigor and utility: mitigating cognitive biases in LLMs for multiple-choice questions
finding: Some bias-like shortcuts help efficiency; allowing abstention and moderating heuristics improves accuracy.
numbers: BRU dataset built with experts; tested GPT-4, Gemini, LLaMA-3-70B. Exact gains not extracted.
limits: Numbers not transcribed this session.
agent_relevance: Allow an explicit abstain option instead of forcing a choice.

source: Kuhberger (2023): threshold test for framing (prospect theory vs rivals)
finding: Prospect theory predicts both halves of the framing pattern, but studies often show only one half; the author lists rival accounts.
numbers: Worked example in the review: 10 of 30 chose the sure gain in the gain frame (not above 50%, chi2=3.33, p=.068) but only 3 of 30 chose the sure loss.
limits: Illustrative example, not a data set.
agent_relevance: Check the effect in both frames separately.

source: Gigerenzer and Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making
finding: Not opened (blocked). Rival view: heuristics are often accurate in uncertain environments.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Do not label every shortcut a bug.

source: Kahneman and Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Not opened (blocked). Joint paper of the two camps: intuition is trustworthy only in regular environments with long feedback.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Gate intuitive answers by whether the domain gives valid cues and feedback.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: Not opened (blocked). Title claims training with feedback reduced bias.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Training with feedback may beat instruction alone.
